title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated deepfake content was used to fabricate a news article featuring recognisable public figures, a Reserve Bank governor and a finance presenter, in order to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure occurred at the distribution layer of the open web, where synthetic media can be published and circulated without any verification of the identities depicted or the claims made. Catching it would have required either platform-level detection of AI-generated impersonation content before publication, or rapid takedown systems capable of acting before the material reached potential investors.

The pattern described by ASIC is not an isolated incident but part of a documented rise in coordinated deception infrastructure, combining fake articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements into a single persuasion environment. The regulator's own figures show a sharp increase in the volume of such scams removed, which indicates the problem is scaling faster than removal efforts.

What is not established is whether any specific individuals were defrauded by this particular fake article, who produced it, or whether the platform named in it, Boulder Sparhaven, was operated by identifiable actors.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, where she allegedly stormed out over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. This fabricated story exemplifies a growing scam trend that uses artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring well-known Australians to promote fraudulent investments. ASIC reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent online.

According to ASIC's latest research, scammers are constructing elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, websites, and advertisements to lure investors. Last year, the regulator took down 19,400 scams, representing a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC advises consumers to verify financial services licenses and check ASIC's public registers before investing, while Kohler argues that platforms distributing such content should face heavy fines.
